title: The 7 Habits That Quietly Multiply Your Luck (According to 25 Years of Research)
author: Is Public Speaking
summary: This article reports on Conor Neill's twenty-five-year research into what makes some people consistently luckier than others — and argues that luck, far from being random, flows through people via conversation, determined by who you talk to and how consistently you expand that circle. Neill, a professor at IESE Business School, identifies seven habits that reliably multiply luck: meeting one new person every week (turned into a calendared commitment, not a nice-to-have); showing up reliably (consistency over intensity as a trust-building mechanism); asking better questions (shifting from 'How are you?' to 'What are you working on?'); sharing what you're working on (making your current projects visible so others can connect you to relevant people); being genuinely helpful with no agenda; following through on small commitments; and expanding conversations into context (finding what's actually interesting about the other person's situation). The article presents these as learnable systems, not personality traits — the point is that lucky people are not different in kind but in the specificity and consistency of how they maintain the conversational infrastructure through which opportunity flows.
points: Luck flows through people by conversation: the people you talk to determine the opportunities you find, which means the most direct lever for changing your luck is deliberately expanding and diversifying who you talk to, not waiting for serendipity.

Meeting one new person per week, turned into a calendared recurring commitment rather than a nice-to-have, is Neill's highest-leverage single habit — over 25 years, the majority of his most important career turns began with a conversation with someone he did not know the week before.

Showing up consistently is the trust-building mechanism that determines whether others think of you when an opportunity appears: consistency over intensity is what signals reliability, and it is reliability that makes you the person someone calls when they have something to share.

Asking 'What are you working on?' instead of 'How are you?' moves conversation from social filler to genuine information exchange — the kind of exchange that creates the mutual visibility through which opportunity actually travels.

The article's most important reframe is that these are systems, not personality traits: people who appear naturally lucky are not more extroverted or more charismatic — they are running a more consistent and more deliberate process of conversational maintenance.
quotes: Why some people seem to get lucky constantly There is a pattern most people notice in others long before they notice it in themselves. Some people appear to be luckier than everyone around them — not once, but repeatedly.
His conclusion, delivered plainly, is that luck is not random. Keep talking to the same people, and you will keep finding the same opportunities.
Someone gave him a simple piece of advice: meet one new person every week. He put it on his calendar as a recurring commitment, not a nice-to-have.
Set aside weekly time to meet someone new, attend a gathering, or reach out to someone whose work you admire. Ask yourself one question: who is the one person it would be useful to meet this week?
This is not a criticism of loyalty or long friendships — it is a statement about how opportunity actually moves. The people around you carry a fixed set of possibilities in their network.
Rotating the room you are speaking into is one of the simplest ways to change the range of what can happen to you next. Change the room If you want different luck, walk into different rooms.
Most of the time, changing the room is a smaller act than people imagine. The first three habits build the surface layer — who you meet, how often, and where.
